entities.name: Otbert of Liège
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Otbert of Liège, who served as Prince-Bishop of Liège from 1091 until his death on February 7, 1119, emerged as a pivotal ecclesiastical and political figure in the Lower Lotharingia region during a period defined by the Investiture Controversy and the burgeoning crusading movement. His tenure solidified the temporal power of the Prince-Bishopric, transforming Liège into a significant regional player and a key financial hub for the First Crusade. A staunch loyalist of Emperor Henry IV, Otbert deftly navigated the complex power dynamics of the Holy Roman Empire, using imperial favor to expand his territorial holdings and influence within the Meuse-Rhine region.

Otbert's most notable contribution was his instrumental role in financing the First Crusade. Lacking personal wealth, he mortgaged the Church of Liège's considerable assets, including its rich treasury and vast estates, to Jewish financiers in Mainz and Cologne. This audacious act raised a substantial sum, estimated at 1,300 marks of silver, which was then loaned to Godfrey of Bouillon, Duke of Lower Lotharingia, enabling him to equip and lead a significant contingent of crusaders to the Holy Land in 1096. Beyond this, Otbert was an active expansionist, acquiring the County of Grevenbroich in 1096 and the Duchy of Bouillon in 1099, the latter from Godfrey's brother Eustace III of Boulogne, further consolidating Liège's secular authority and strategic importance.

entities.summary:
Otbert, Prince-Bishop of Liège from 1091 to 1119, emerged as a pivotal figure in the political and ecclesiastical landscape of the late 11th and early 12th centuries, notably for his unwavering loyalty to the Salian emperors amidst the Investiture Controversy and his instrumental role in financing the First Crusade. His episcopate marked a period of significant territorial expansion and consolidation for the Prince-Bishopric of Liège, transforming it into a formidable regional power within the Holy Roman Empire. Operating from the strategically vital Meuse-Rhine region, Otbert navigated complex alliances and conflicts, directly influencing the trajectory of both imperial and crusading endeavors.

Elected to the see of Liège in 1091, Otbert quickly aligned himself with Emperor Henry IV, becoming one of his most trusted and active supporters against the papacy and its allies. This loyalty was vividly demonstrated by his substantial financial contributions to the First Crusade, which were critical in enabling Godfrey of Bouillon, Duke of Lower Lorraine, to equip his contingent for the journey to the Holy Land in 1096. Otbert's personal treasury and the resources of his bishopric were leveraged to support the expedition, a testament to his commitment to imperial policy and perhaps a shrewd calculation to redirect bellicose nobles. Beyond crusader finance, Otbert aggressively pursued territorial gains, acquiring the county of Brunengeruz and the lordship of Amay in 1101, and the county of Grez in 1107, thereby expanding Liège's feudal domain and economic base.
